title: The Frontier AI Inference Cloud for Agents — Byung-Gon (Gon) Chun, FriendliAI
talk_summary: FriendliAI argues agent workloads differ from chat because tasks involve long, growing contexts and many LLM/tool loops, so inference should optimize end-to-end task latency via prefix caching, KV-cache management, cache-aware routing, and agent-aware scheduling. It also claims open-weight models like GLM 5.2 are now good enough for many coding-agent tasks at much lower cost, though the cost example is vendor marketing and internally inconsistent.

takeaways.technique: Open-weight routing for low-risk agent work
takeaways.what_they_do: They run the same coding-agent task on an open-weight GLM model and a frontier closed model, claiming both outputs are usable while the open-weight model is far cheaper.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Opus 4.8 cost about a $150 GLM 5.2 unfriendly AI cost 27 cents
takeaways.numbers: Vendor claim: Opus 4.8 ~$150 vs GLM 5.2 $0.27 for same task; speaker says ~5.6x cheaper, but $150/$0.27 is ~555x—verify.

takeaways.technique: Stable prompt prefix for prefix caching
takeaways.what_they_do: Agent steps share a large prefix; cache KV for that prefix once and process only the new suffix on later steps.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Consecutive agent steps usually share a huge prefix.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of round-robin load balancing, route requests to a backend that already has the prefix cached while still balancing load.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It sends a request to part that already has the right prefix cached

takeaways.what_they_do: Optimize end-to-end task completion rather than individual LLM call latency; an agent-aware scheduler can preempt or prefetch based on task context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the real metric is end to end test latency, not a single request latency.
